items.label: A
items.critique: Stock-phrase bounty speech ('dead or alive', 'savage scum', 'lose no sleep fretting about his soul'), double-dash punctuation and exact gold sums: pure Westwood melodrama with easy humour.

items.label: B
items.critique: Long first speech packs in a back-story, a deduction ('You'll know if he has') and a trap warning. The comic student ('second year, maybe third', the broom) is a modern, knowing kind of whimsy.

items.label: C
items.critique: Plain enough, but the second asker's family plot, with several persons, a hostage and a back-door key, is too intricate. The muted 'cap' outcome ('Well... thanks for going up there for him') is an understated grief Westwood never writes.

items.label: D
items.critique: Earnest kidnapped-maiden pleading, 'the menfolk cannot live without us', the hungry-Ogre stomach joke and the accept/decline pair are Westwood's simple yes/no quest shape.

items.label: E
items.critique: Breathless exclamations, a slightly awkward comma ('[Place], the village north of here and kidnapped') and near-identical generic thanks ('token of my appreciation'): flat, but typical of Westwood's filler NPCs.

items.label: F
items.critique: Vivid setting detail (reed-cutters, cutting platform, frog-boys, a fine paid in frogs) and long run-on comic speeches. Westwood's quirk is broader and shorter, with less invented local colour.

items.label: G
items.critique: Pay-chest-plus-dead-courier and a partner-turned-animal with a wand left in a cart: elaborate setup, 'Hmmm... Yes. You'll do.' theatre and a hand-off to another NPC, all built to the same template as J.

items.label: H
items.critique: Terse officialdom ('you'll need official sponsorship'), a non-sequitur apple-orchard urchin errand, 'ruby key' and a sulky refusal line read as authentic Westwood quest-chain dialogue.

items.label: I
items.critique: Short, breezy smuggler talk ('Oh, bah!', 'give ya one of the enchanted shields'), reward and key named plainly, a light joke about dodging responsibilities: Westwood's chapter-town voice.

items.label: J
items.critique: Mirrors G's pay-chest and enchanted-partner template. Grammar slips ('Ambushes ... is a daily occurrence', 'they're mean and hungry lot') look like editing seams rather than Westwood's breathlessness, and the flue-key wry ending is too knowing.

tells: The new quests lean on templates (a stolen pay or tithe chest with a missing courier; a partner turned into an animal, the wand left elsewhere) and give side quests more named people and plot links than Westwood does.

The new first speeches pack setting detail, back-story, a deduction and a warning into one breath. Westwood's asks are shorter, state the trouble and the reward plainly, and often split accept and decline into separate replies.

The new humour is dry and specific (dialectal craft words, invented local customs, deadpan asides). Westwood's is broad, exclamatory and stock-phrased ('savage scum', 'lose no sleep', 'token of my appreciation').
The new outcomes add quiet grief or understatement ('Well... thanks for going up there') and hand-offs to the next NPC. Westwood's thanks are effusive, generic and name the gold sum.
Westwood's flaws are naive (repetitive thanks, a clumsy comma). The new flaws are agreement slips and stacked clauses inside otherwise polished prose.
